@ Well, it's, maybe not like we'd hope. We wish for being able to share things or interests, maybe peacefully resolve old baggage. Maybe that happens for some and I really hope that it does.
Both the physical and mental load is substantial if you're the sole caregiver. If one or more you are taking care of have cognitive, mobility, or medical issues, this adds a significant level of care you'll need to provide. If you are also doing the cooking and cleaning, it takes an even higher toll on you.
Mine just would not allow anyone (they'd run them off by the 3rd appointment) but me. If you can get reasonable support lined up or have siblings that pitch in, it could help a great deal and free you up to enjoy some of your time with them.

snippet.textDisplay: I was in this situation (siblings live in other states) one almost never visited in eleven years. I cared for my Mom (dementia, no mobility) and father (abusive, mobile with personality disorder) until two years before they passed (Mom naturally, father took his life). The last two years, I had to walk away. My oldest sister (well to do), paid for their in home care and visited when she could. The other sister never visited. I went from a very active and healthy 50-60’s year old married lady to a person with heart problems and Graves Disease. I thank God every day for my patient and loving husband. Please make sure you are cared for also! Being strong for years is great and admirable, but you have no idea how long your parents may need your assistance. In home care is wonderful if you can afford it. I could have never walked away if it meant they had to go to a nursing home. I wish the best for you. You are doing the hardest job there is in life. Bless you ♥️ 🤗

snippet.textDisplay:
We had my Mum living with us for the last 7 years of her life (81-88). Thankfully it was a blessing. Our 2 sons (10 and 14 when she came) as well as my husband just loved having her with us. So did i.
Only a few times right towards the end she sometimes became a bit confused. Each time when I explained to her what she'd become muddled about "Yes Mum I did bring you supper 😄", "Yes it is night time and no longer day. Maybe you closed your curtains earlier than usual?" - she would realise her mind wasn't functioning clearly, burst out laughing and say "Oh Darling, am I going bats?!" to which I always replied "Yes! I'm afraid so!".

The funniest was once she rang her bell imperiously at about 3am. I got the fright of my life. I ran down the passage, out of the back door, down the 3 steps (VERY nearly tripping and falling on my face)..to her flat.

I flung open her door. I had imagined that she must've had a fall and broken her hip, and somehow reached the buzzer to the main house.

Yet there she was, sitting straight up in bed, with her hands neatly in her lap.

"I want biscuits!" she declared. I went through to her little kitchen, made her a pot of tea and brought her 3 biscuits. She took a bite of the first one, a sip of her tea, then looked over the rim of her teacup with her big dark brown eyes.

I was sitting on her bed.

Suddenly she said "Oh my darling, am I being ridiculous? Did I wake you? I am SO sorry!".

We both laughed and laughed. She had become increasingly sweet-natured as she grew older. Not that she'd ever been mean. I had just not been close to her at ALL while growing up.

So I was actually grateful for those last years.

We did have to get a carer in to help me to care for her 3x a week in the morning.

I would not have managed to care for her if she was incontinent.

When my one brother had a dreadful aggressive cancer, after 4 mths we could not help him to the bathroom any more: he was 6'4", and he became extremely weak. He had to go into hospital. The last two months he spent in a wonderful old age home.

I fully agree and understand what you are all saying here. My husband and I both turn 66 this year. We have spent the last year gradually re-painting the same house to sell it, sorting through our possessions, giving things away6, throwing others out, and I've sold a few things and been surprised at how much I earned for them.

I gave my precious guitar away 2 weeks ago to our painter - and he lit up like a beacon! He plays beautifully, and it was definitely the right thing to do.

We also both have many many books. We're only shedding a few of those at this point!
My husband has photographed and "digitised" ALL our photos, and our children's art, and his diaries (mine are private! 😄).
He has shredded over 50 bags of papers, drawings etc.
We have kept the VERY precious ones.

SO one day when we die, our sons will not have to spend months and months wading through everything, as my husband has been doing over years.

He doesn't resent it, but is motivated to avert our sons being landed in a similar stew.

After we've moved to a smaller flat, if one of requires care, we have found a carehome that is not exorbitant and where the staff are apparently skilled and patient.
Sounds perfect to me.
I just pray that until the day we die both of recognise our children and are able to express our love and say a proper goodbye ♥️❤️

snippet.textDisplay: My mother turns 99 in two short months. I’m 71. She doesn’t live with me (thank Heavens!) but went into care after battling a couple of illnesses almost 3 1/2 years ago. I have looked after her for 17 years, getting her to all of her medical appointments, picking up groceries, helping her do her banking, etc and have been responsible for her healthcare and finances for 13 years since she first went into assisted living. She began showing signs of dementia a couple of years after that and also was experiencing more hearing loss. Now she is deaf, fully into dementia and in a wheelchair. Visiting her is no longer enjoyable and hasn’t been for a few years. She knows me but is oblivious to everything going on around her. I can’t imagine what it’s like for her to be living such a life. For me, it’s exhausting. Make no mistake, even though a family member isn’t looking after an elderly parent or family member personally, it is still emotionally and sometimes physically exhausting. In the ensuing years since my mother went into assisted living, I’ve had to pack up her belongings and move some items to my home and move a few items to her assisted living suite, empty her house of any other items in her store room, supervise the sale of her house, deal with the assisted living management and staff on my mother’s behalf (she didn’t want to do anything much, especially make big decisions, for herself) regarding her in-house supports etc. I’ve seen her through four surgeries and countless other appointments. I’ve sorted out and supervised financial and investment concerns for her, stored all manner of tax, finance, investment and medical information for her in multiple bankers boxes at my small home (which take up a lot of room!) and have run around getting her toiletries etc as well as visiting her regularly and meeting her in the emergency room whenever she’s had a fall and hurt herself. Now I have to meet the dental hygienist each time she comes to clean my mom’s teeth because my mom gets upset and agitated. If I’m there, my mom is calmer during the process. I have looked after my mom diligently for years, and I’ve lost count of how often my life has been put on the back burner in order to deal with her needs. Many people will know that when an elderly person has need of medical attention and such, that the carer has to make decisions and get the needs met because those needs can’t wait. Doctors, nurses, dental hygienists, Care-aids, or whoever, need prompt answers to their questions and decisions made by the person with Power of Attorney. So the family member in charge sacrifices their life regularly for the well being of the elderly person for whom they are responsible. I have my own home to look after as well as my own finances, taxes, grocery shopping etc to take care of but all of that isn’t taken into account by others. What I also know is that often, the designated carer gets little help if any from other family members. I’ve seen and heard about this time and again and it happened to me. My late brother did very little to help, rarely even offered. He was running a business with his wife but I often wondered it he kept working to avoid having to help with his mother and preferred to leave me carrying the full load alone. Am I tired out, emotionally and physically worn down? You bet I am! I’ve had my own health issues to deal with for the last 4 years or so and this makes looking after my mom even more difficult. Don’t ever let anyone tell you that it’s not so tough to care for a parent if your parent is in full care. That’s not only a lie, it’s an insult! 😒🇨🇦

Doctors, nurses, dental hygienists, Care-aids, or whoever, need prompt answers to their questions and decisions made by the person with Power of Attorney. So the family member in charge sacrifices their life regularly for the well being of the elderly person for whom they are responsible. I have my own home to look after as well as my own finances, taxes, grocery shopping etc to take care of but all of that isn’t taken into account by others. What I also know is that often, the designated carer gets little help if any from other family members. I’ve seen and heard about this time and again and it happened to me. My late brother did very little to help, rarely even offered. He was running a business with his wife but I often wondered it he kept working to avoid having to help with his mother and preferred to leave me carrying the full load alone. Am I tired out, emotionally and physically worn down? You bet I am! I’ve had my own health issues to deal with for the last 4 years or so and this makes looking after my mom even more difficult. Don’t ever let anyone tell you that it’s not so tough to care for a parent if your parent is in full care. That’s not only a lie, it’s an insult! 😒🇨🇦

snippet.textDisplay: I have seen people comment about how awful every single assisted living facility is.  That is simply not true.  The one my mom is in is amazing.  I could not watch my mother every single second of the day and she was always getting into things.  She loved heat and would open the oven door when I was baking, just to feel the heat. I did what was best for my mom and for my family and my own sanity and health.  It was not sustainable for me so I did what was needed.  Now I have to work at not feeling guilty, but I still know I did the right thing.

My mom moved in with me when she turned 82. I was so fortunate that she was in good shape and had good health.. but she was starting to have mobility issues. I remodeled her bathroom and made sure it was totally handicap accessible… she called it her spa! She remained able to care for her own hygiene , dress herself and feed herself. When she turned 92 she had a stroke , she spent a week in the hospital and then rehab. Little did I know that it would lead to her passing. The doctors advised that I put her in a nursing home for hospice care. My mother was a nurse for 55 years when she retired. I went to visit the nursing homes that were recommended to me. I could not do it… I chose to bring her home for hospice. Together with my family we took total care of her.. she could not walk, talk or even feed herself. There wasn’t a day that I did not cry my eyes out and pray for our Lord and Savior to bring her home. Having her there with me was a beautiful gift that I will always be thankful for. Mom passed 23 days after bringing her home. We didn’t do everything perfect but we did the best we could for that sweet loving soul.
It truly is not for everyone to take on.. believe me I prayed to God to give me the strength to see it through.
There is so much truth in this video… it will be the hardest thing you will ever do both physically and mentally.
Depending on your relationship, taking care of a parent has many rewards. But taking care of yourself is equally just as important.

You’re not alone in feeling this way. So many people are expected to become caregivers to the very people who hurt them, neglected them, or showed them little care — and then everyone acts like it’s just your job now. That kind of emotional whiplash is real, and it cuts deep.

It makes sense that you’re feeling resentment. It doesn’t make you a bad person — it makes you a human being with a history. Your past matters. Your boundaries matter.

And please — don’t feel guilty for protecting your peace, your health, or your finances. You have the right to care for yourself. You are allowed to say ‘no,’ or ‘not like this,’ or ‘I need help.’ You can still be a compassionate person and draw a line to keep from drowning.

This isn’t about abandoning anyone — it’s about not abandoning yourself. And that matters too.

snippet.textDisplay: I have lived through everything you're talking about. I cared for my elderly mother while she went through hospice. My mom had moved in with us because she could no longer care for a house. I didn't realize until sometime later she was having cognitive issues as well as physical illness. When you have children, it's a given that they'll be in diapers for the first couple of years. When you have to put your parent in diapers, it's heartbreaking. You know they aren't going to grow out of it, and you watch the person that you looked up to and loved your whole life turn into this other person you don't know anymore. While my mother began to develop dementia, she remembered who I was up until the end. She may not have always been able to remember my name, but she remembered I was her daughter. Thank you for posting this. Sometimes you suffer tremendous guilt when you get upset with them or lose your patience. You can often resent being put in the position of caregiver because you don't always feel up to it. But I'm grateful every day that I was there for my mother. You know they aren't going to grow out of it, and you watch the person that you looked up to and loved your whole life turn into this other person you don't know anymore. While my mother began to develop dementia, she remembered who I was up until the end. She may not have always been able to remember my name, but she remembered I was her daughter. Thank you for posting this. Sometimes you suffer tremendous guilt when you get upset with them or lose your patience. I wouldn't have traded those last couple of months for anything no matter how difficult it was.

snippet.textDisplay: I'm an occupational therapist and this is the most realistic video I've seen on this topic. In 2019, I relocated from California back to my hometown of Philadelphia to help care for my Father, who had dementia. I knew my mother wouldn't be able to handle him by herself. With the help of a friend of mine, who's a hospice nurse, we were able to keep him home until two weeks before he died in February 2022. Even with my healthcare experience, it was a challenging situation. My experience has been that the caregiving usually falls on the most responsible sibling. If you're lucky, you'll have two siblings who will help out. Everyone else looks the other way, living their lives and pretending that life is great. If the family is dysfunctional, all the cracks will show. I think the hardest thing is you don't know how long it will go on for. Caring for the elderly shows just how broken American culture is. It's all good till you can't care for yourself. Then it's a different story. People don't want to face this reality and therefore it falls on one or two responsible people to do all the work.

snippet.textDisplay:
MUST READ! So true. There are so many problems. Here is a typical day for me:
Keep in mind I am an only child and there is no other family. I am in my 50's, the parent in their 90's. We do get help from the State and SS so I am able to be here.
1. They wake up at any odd hour yelling to go to the bathroom.

2. I go in and have to lift the person up from behind in order to get up out of bed. They need help getting up at other times also.
3. They need help getting night clothing off before going to the bathroom, like leg warmers, thick socks, and so on.
4. They sit up then and gather a few items from the nightstand. There are 3 glass cases, each with a different item that they feel they must take to bed and back with them.... so an invisible enemy does not steal them. Paranoia and delusions: yes.
5. They use a walker to bulldoze their way around and then get to the toilet. They have severe OCD so they take forever with each task. They put toilet paper on the toilet seat as a seat cover, even though I, the daughter, am the only other person who uses it. They sit and do their business. They wear several layers. An underwear, with a pad. A set of folded paper towel. A diaper. Two pairs of pants. One pair of socks. If any one of these is soiled, it all has to come off which they can't do by themselves. Usually at least one of them is so it all needs to go off and some in the wash. They sit there for a time with a mirror, picking at little things. Finally they get up, dropping most of the toilet paper on the seat to the floor. They grab another small piece of toilet paper... to flush the toilet! Oh, and that falls to the ground as well. They get up and shuffle over to the sink while I pick up all the pieces of wasted TP with a grabber. They wash their hands.... for half an hour. Then, they dry their hands... for another half hour. But... you can't rush them. The faucet handles are slathered in soap so later I wipe them down. They shuffle back to the bedroom where I put all the clean clothes back on and new sets of the items.
6. The bed... has about six blankets on that are slippery so the bed is a mess each morning. They need so many layers of everything and we take sweaters, polar hats, shawls and stuff to the living room when all else is done.
7. They sit and turn on the space heater.... which is on a LOT. Even though it's not that cold. It is also expensive. I fix the meal and do the dishes several times a day. They want tea... again. It got cold... again. It is in a thermus, but they forget to put the lid on and would rather have it off... because... it's too hot.
8. After a meal sometimes they get diarrhea. And it is no small amount. They make it to the toilet as fast as they can, but it still gets everywhere. They can't clean themselves, or the mess left behind that is all over the toilet and the floor. They can even slip in it. So I get to deal with it all, after putting a fresh set of everything on already a little while ago. So it's a new set of everything after the major wipe down and cleaning, sanitizing the area.
9. They make a mess everywhere. They leave little pieces of trash here and there. I do all the housework as it is, laundry, etc. etc. I do bring blankets and warm drinks. I am fine with that and even enjoy it and don't complain about the typical needs, but it's the attitude that is the killer.
10. They insist on putting their contact lenses in. They lose one. But it wasn't them, someone is sneaking in and stealing them. They want to buy more. They spent a lot on lenses as it is. They have old ones but with damage, they insist on using them anyway, they scream in pain, can't get them out, finally do, one gets lost, and it starts all over again.
11. They used to leave things on the stove that would burn due to early dementia. After I'd gone to bed. Trying to get them in bed before me was impossible. If I go on errands I worry about this also. Putting things in the oven 'to dry,' leaving faucets running while doing hand laundry and the sink would run over. One day the house was filled with smoke. The only thing that sinks in is if you get really mad and yell. If they were bed ridden, my life would have been easier!
12. They don't want a traditional bath.
13. Forget about any sort of vacation or travel, decent day off, etc.
14. They have their own version of reality. If they can't push it on you, they get hostile and attack you.
15. They do foolish things and fall down. They have conditions that could lead to broken bones with a fall. I tell them but they don't listen. They can't get up by themselves. I am strong and they are thin so I am able to get them up. But it's not always easy. Sometimes they don't want to use the walker. The cane is not enough. But they have a 'can do' attitude. Great.
16. You can't tell them anything, they won't listen to you... because "you are their child and they are the parent" is in their mind forever.
17. We had to change something at the bank to keep the homecare hours. The parent kept arguing with me about it even though the amount was my money. I finally lost it and yelled and then they cooperated and it turned out okay.
18. I am always worried they will say something wrong at the reassessments due to dementia and we will lose the hours, like "oh no, I don't need any help with that, or this..." etc. They are very 'independent,' and stubborn and delusional about their abilities. And that situation has happened, causing a loss of some hours.
19. Now hallucinations have begun and there are mysterious people in their bedroom at night.
20. Getting them in bed is now easier due to physical decline and lack of enthusiasm for other things, and the person had always been a night owl. So this was a big win.
21. With dementia people argue, get aggressive, don't want to cooperate, and in this case there is also mental illness.
22. There was an illness earlier that caused terrible behavior that was toxic and verbally abusive. I think it would even go physical but they know I am stronger so they don't dare try anything stupid. The attitude would get better and worse. At one point last winter, and we get snow, it was so bad I did not want to run into them in the hallway and I had to go to the bathroom so I went into the backyard with freezing temperatures just to empty my bladder. The snow cleaned up after me. I would rather shiver than deal with the bad attitude.
23. On top of all this, people still look down on caregivers. There is the attitude of 'just' a caregiver, like you are just a servant, maid, slave, second class citizen, etc. It's just some lowly job in their eyes like a janitor, cleaning lady, etc.
24. In public they can turn on the charm, so they always tell me how 'cute' my parent is and so on, because they know so much more about it of course. All my saintly sweetness goes unnoticed by them most of the time. Patience... the patience that is needed, the nerves that are shredded, the stress... my BP went up, I have other health conditions due to the stress that I haven't had in over a decade, and so on.
25. It just goes on and on and on. The worst combination is when they are still physically able but not mentally. That's when they can start wandering outside at night and stuff. That... did not occur. There are symptoms of nearing death but in this case it is drawn out longer than the time estimates given. For some it goes on for decades depending on when dementia sets in. The worst aggravation is the bad behavior. The accusations. The irrationality and hostility and even harassment. That stuff is what takes such an emotional toll. I could live with the rest, but it is due to that that I am at my wits end! Now I even have to worry about the social safety nets breaking due to doge and then we would be stranded. Because this wasn't already stressful enough. Kids grow up pretty quick, but this can last decades and only gets worse. The physical demands, time demands, need for supervision, they can hardly be left alone, managing them such as redirecting their attention away from something setting them off, etc. It's like having a special needs kid mentally and physically who thinks they are in charge. No one understands that I am praying for this to end. Once life gets to that point it is no longer a quality life. They are human and I don't believe in euthanasia or stuff, but I would not want to get to this point. There is no money for a nursing home either. When conversations used to be a thing, all they would talk about was the bad stuff, the bad people in their life and what they did in the past, which I heard hundreds of times, and it wasn't even all true. Yes.. the little joys!
There is probably more that I am forgetting but you get the picture by now I would imagine and you probably want to forget it and run. Lol

They shuffle back to the bedroom where I put all the clean clothes back on and new sets of the items.  
6.  The bed... has about six blankets on that are slippery so the bed is a mess each morning.  They need so many layers of everything and we take sweaters, polar hats, shawls and stuff to the living room when all else is done.
7.  They sit and turn on the space heater.... which is on a LOT.  Even though it's not that cold.  It is also expensive.  I fix the meal and do the dishes several times a day.  They want tea... again.  It got cold... again.  It is in a thermus, but they forget to put the lid on and would rather have it off... because... it's too hot.  
8.  After a meal sometimes they get diarrhea.  And it is no small amount.  They make it to the toilet as fast as they can, but it still gets everywhere.  They can't clean themselves, or the mess left behind that is all over the toilet and the floor.  They can even slip in it.  So I get to deal with it all, after putting a fresh set of everything on already a little while ago.  So it's a new set of everything after the major wipe down and cleaning, sanitizing the area.
9.  They make a mess everywhere.  They leave little pieces of trash here and there.  I do all the housework as it is, laundry, etc. etc.  I do bring blankets and warm drinks.  I am fine with that and even enjoy it and don't complain about the typical needs, but it's the attitude that is the killer.
10.  They insist on putting their contact lenses in.  They lose one.  But it wasn't them, someone is sneaking in and stealing them.  They want to buy more.  They spent a lot on lenses as it is.  They have old ones but with damage, they insist on using them anyway, they scream in pain, can't get them out, finally do, one gets lost, and it starts all over again.
11.  They used to leave things on the stove that would burn due to early dementia.  After I'd gone to bed.  Trying to get them in bed before me was impossible.  If I go on errands I worry about this also.  Putting things in the oven 'to dry,' leaving faucets running while doing hand laundry and the sink would run over.  One day the house was filled with smoke.  The only thing that sinks in is if you get really mad and yell.  If they were bed ridden, my life would have been easier!
12.  They don't want a traditional bath.  
13.  Forget about any sort of vacation or travel, decent day off, etc.
14.  They have their own version of reality.  If they can't push it on you, they get hostile and attack you.
15.  They do foolish things and fall down.  They have conditions that could lead to broken bones with a fall.  I tell them but they don't listen.  They can't get up by themselves.  I am strong and they are thin so I am able to get them up.  But it's not always easy.  Sometimes they don't want to use the walker.  The cane is not enough.  But they have a 'can do' attitude.  Great.
16.  You can't tell them anything, they won't listen to you... because "you are their child and they are the parent" is in their mind forever.
17.  We had to change something at the bank to keep the homecare hours.  The parent kept arguing with me about it even though the amount was my money.  I finally lost it and yelled and then they cooperated and it turned out okay.
18.  I am always worried they will say something wrong at the reassessments due to dementia and we will lose the hours, like "oh no, I don't need any help with that, or this..." etc.   They are very 'independent,' and stubborn and delusional about their abilities.  And that situation has happened, causing a loss of some hours.
19.  Now hallucinations have begun and there are mysterious people in their bedroom at night.
20.  Getting them in bed is now easier due to physical decline and lack of enthusiasm for other things, and the person had always been a night owl.  So this was a big win.
21.  With dementia people argue, get aggressive, don't want to cooperate, and in this case there is also mental illness.
22.  There was an illness earlier that caused terrible behavior that was toxic and verbally abusive.  I think it would even go physical but they know I am stronger so they don't dare try anything stupid.  The attitude would get better and worse.  At one point last winter, and we get snow, it was so bad I did not want to run into them in the hallway and I had to go to the bathroom so I went into the backyard with freezing temperatures just to empty my bladder.  The snow cleaned up after me.  I would rather shiver than deal with the bad attitude.
23.  On top of all this, people still look down on caregivers.  There is the attitude of 'just' a caregiver, like you are just a servant, maid, slave, second class citizen, etc.  It's just some lowly job in their eyes like a janitor, cleaning lady, etc.
24.  In public they can turn on the charm, so they always tell me how 'cute' my parent is and so on, because they know so much more about it of course.  All my saintly sweetness goes unnoticed by them most of the time.  Patience... the patience that is needed, the nerves that are shredded, the stress... my BP went up, I have other health conditions due to the stress that I haven't had in over a decade, and so on.  
25.  It just goes on and on and on.  The worst combination is when they are still physically able but not mentally.  That's when they can start wandering outside at night and stuff.  That... did not occur.   There are symptoms of nearing death but in this case it is drawn out longer than the time estimates given.  For some it goes on for decades depending on when dementia sets in.  The worst aggravation is the bad behavior.  The accusations.  The irrationality and hostility and even harassment.  That stuff is what takes such an emotional toll.  I could live with the rest, but it is due to that that I am at my wits end!  Now I even have to worry about the social safety nets breaking due to doge and then we would be stranded.  Because this wasn't already stressful enough.  Kids grow up pretty quick, but this can last decades and only gets worse.  The physical demands, time demands, need for supervision, they can hardly be left alone, managing them such as redirecting their attention away from something setting them off, etc.  It's like having a special needs kid mentally and physically who thinks they are in charge.  No one understands that I am praying for this to end.  Once life gets to that point it is no longer a quality life.  They are human and I don't believe in euthanasia or stuff, but I would not want to get to this point.  There is no money for a nursing home either.   When conversations used to be a thing, all they would talk about was the bad stuff, the bad people in their life and what they did in the past, which I heard hundreds of times, and it wasn't even all true.  Yes.. the little joys!
There is probably more that I am forgetting but you get the picture by now I would imagine and you probably want to forget it and run.  Lol

snippet.textDisplay: My sister and I had to split care between our parents because my father and I were estranged from years back. She took on his care and I'm pretty sure she thought I was going to have it worse with our mom. Mom died suddenly at home, probably from a slow suicide because she refused to eat and was again engaging in the substance abuse that had been off and on since she was young. Our dad developed Alzheimer's. I truly believe my sister was on her way to having a mental breakdown when she was finally able to get him into a dementia unit at a local nursing home. Not only was she caring for him but also having to take care of the third wife because this person had decided years earlier she no longer wanted to get out of bed each day. My father had been caring for her since that time until he was no longer able to do so. They both went to the same facility. My father, who had been a social introvert for most of his life suddenly turned into the life of the party the two years he was there. He thrived in the environment, probably because he was eating regular meals and taking his medications like he should. He passed away in 2023 after developing a septic UTI. The staff told my sister they knew something was wrong when he left a party early to go lie down in his room. To them, that was uncharacteristic behavior. To us, we would have just thought his dementia was easing off 😂. Never, ever, ever feel guilty for putting your parent somewhere they will be safer. Do not allow anyone to tell you they would never do this to their parents unless you know they didn't. I did my best to support my sister through this and today we have a better relationship then we had as kids simply because we were able to overcome past grievances and move forward when we were faced with these situations. But it isn't like that for everyone. We were just lucky and blessed. Not everyone has that support

snippet.textDisplay: I am a caregiver to my parents. I am a 59 year old divorced mother of 2 grown boys. I had been an empty nester for about 2 years when I was asked to retire early from my teaching career, sell my house, and move to another state to care for my mom with dementia and my dad with cancer. My brother is still married so it mae sense that I should be the one to help. My youngest was still in college. I sold my home, gave up full retirement, and moved to care for mom and dad. I have been here 19 months now. I left a vibrant area to move to a rural area. I miss my old life. I miss my own space. I miss my friends. I had a nestegg from the sale of my home, but it is quickly dwindling away with one still in college and no paycheck coming in. Because I left my job early, I can not draw retirement until age 60. It has been hard! Dementia is such a terrible disease. My mother was so energetic and so full of life. She did everything right - she took care of herself - never drank or smoked, walked 10 miles a day, and ate healthy. To see this happen to her is so cruel. Why take care of yourself?! It is hard for me to even remember who she was. My dad was the same as mom, always eating healthy and very athletic - never drank or smoked. I get to watch him fight cancer and the evils of chemo. My kids don't come visit anymore because this isn't their home, and they say it is "depressing." I have decided that I want to be in a nursing home if I get to this point. I also want to leave my entire body to science - no burial and no funeral! This Christmas was the first one that I had without my kids. I wonder how long my life will be on hold and if I will even have a life after this.

snippet.textDisplay: I was 48 in 2018 (daughter) when my father's illness reached the point where he could not toilet by himself anymore.  He did not have dementia.  He had his full mental capacities and in a way, that made it worse.  Having to change his diaper was extremely traumatic for me.  I only had to do it on the weekends when I went to his home to give his wife (not my mother) a break.  My brother was a truck driver and was never around.  I told my brother about it, how it felt like a violation and he paid for home health care workers to come in for several days a week for several hours and that was a game changer for me and my father's wife. Having them meant that during the week, his wife could get more time to herself and to do other things and only had to change him/bathe etc. about two days a week instead of five (she was in her mid 60s) and I didn't have to change him anymore on the weekends because the home health workers were there to do it.  Since my dad was in his full right mind, it was the hardest thing to tell him that I just couldn't do it.  I would do everything else on the weekends: cook meals for the week, clean the whole house, wash dishes, go grocery shopping, run other errands, but I just couldn't change his diaper anymore.  He said he understood and I hope he really did.  He passed away in 2019.

snippet.textDisplay: Not sure how things work in the States but in the UK, if you have less than @£23k in savings, social services picks up the tab for care costs BUT they claim it back when your house is sold if you own one. People who have worked hard to own their own home to leave something to their kids don't ... even if they've paid a ton of taxes over their lifetime. It's a very unequal system but who said life is fair?! At least there's a safety net in this country which is something but we have the same problems here with staff shortages.

snippet.textDisplay: I think the hardest part was the shortage of family support. I had Ovarian Carcinoma, two major operations and only twelve days later, found out no-one had been to see my mother for twelve days! I wasn't supposed to even touch a vacuum cleaner for three months but it was right back to 'business as usual'. With criticism on top! I'm not sorry though because I know I did my best for my beloved mother, and gave it all I had, even if it was never enough. Watching a loved one die by inches with dementia was one of the most heartbreaking things I have ever endured. When she eventually died I was so exhausted I slept for most of the next six months, and once woke up with my face in my dinner! 'Loved you so much, mom. ❤❤❤

snippet.textDisplay:
@SoloSecondHalf it’s seeing the person you knew fading away in front of your eyes. Sitting in the house you were raised in, bathing your mother in the bath she used to bathe you in, seeing life going full circle and crying in silence at the loss which has not yet been totally lost. You are left caring for the shell of a person who doesn’t want to be there, having the conversation ‘you will have to wait your turn, I cannot help you’. In many ways we were very lucky, COVID released us both before dementia stripped her entirely of her dignity and took years from my life.
I just hang onto the hope that assisted dying happens before it’s my turn.
